uncited: Frustum and Visibility Culling methods optimize volume rendering by identifying and discarding geometry that does not contribute to the final image, thereby reducing computational load.
Unlike [Octree and Tree Traversal](4134-octree-and-tree-traversal.md) which focuses on hierarchical descent, these methods focus on spatial containment relative to the camera.
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of hierarchical descent and ascent.
The traversal begins at the root of the octree and determines which of the eight children (octants) the ray intersects.
**Empty Space Skipping:** If the selected child is marked as empty (or uniform), the traversal skips the subtree.
**Backtracking:** Because octrees are sparse and irregular, traversal often requires backtracking to the parent node when a ray exits a subtree or encounters an empty branch.
This is implemented using an explicit stack (on GPU) or recursion (on CPU) [S4, S6, S8, unofficial].
The concept of culling visible geometry is fundamental to computer graphics.
In the context of volume rendering, early approaches relied on explicit pre-passes to determine the "working set" of bricks or voxels.

The specific techniques described in the subtopics represent specialized applications of these principles to different data structures (octrees, splats, bounding-sphere trees) and rendering paradigms (rasterization, ray-casting).
